title: श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता — अर्जुनविषादयोगः
titleEn: The Bhagavad Gītā — Chapter 1: Arjuna's Despair
draftNote: Pilot chapter (2026-09-15): first Sanskrit text in Lectorium and first use of the words model for an alphabetic script, to prove the sandhi-split reading layer. Chapters 2–18 to follow by scheduled runs once the presentation is approved.
source: Text: the received (vulgate) text of the Bhagavadgītā, Mahābhārata 6.23–40, as read by Śaṅkara's commentary. Devanagari from Sanskrit Wikisource (भगवद्गीता/अर्जुनविषादयोगः), collated verse by verse against the GRETIL e-text of the Bhagavadgītā with Śaṅkara's commentary (input Gaudiya Grantha Mandira); the four discrepancies are adjudicated in the notes (1.8, 1.22, 1.44; 1.5 and 1.15 differ only in anusvāra vs. class nasal). Collation against a pre-1930 printed edition is still to be done and is noted as pending. Transliteration: IAST. The reading under each word gives the words with sandhi undone and compound members hyphenated, in the manner of the traditional pada-pāṭha. Pronunciation convention: classical Sanskrit as described in Whitney's Sanskrit Grammar (1889), the standard recitation pronunciation; no audio yet. Translations made fresh from the Sanskrit with Monier-Williams (1899) and Apte (1890); no modern translation consulted.
about: The Bhagavadgītā, 'the Song of the Lord', is a dialogue of seven hundred verses set into the Mahābhārata at the moment before the great battle of Kurukṣetra. Chapter 1 is the frame: the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks his minister Sañjaya what is happening on the field; Sañjaya reports Duryodhana's nervous survey of the two armies, the blowing of the war-conches, and Arjuna's request to be driven between the lines to see whom he must fight. Seeing teachers, uncles, cousins and friends on both sides, Arjuna is overcome, lays down his bow and refuses to fight. His despair is the question the rest of the poem answers. The chapter is nearly all names and kinship terms; its value for the reader is that it teaches the two things every Sanskrit page needs first — how words fuse at their edges (sandhi) and how compounds are read backwards from their last member — on the simplest possible content.

sentences.t: धृतराष्ट्र उवाच
sentences.tr: dhṛtarāṣṭra uvāca
sentences.l: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said

morph.gloss: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the blind king of the Kurus, father of the hundred Kauravas (nom. sg.; final -ḥ dropped before the vowel u-)

sentences.t:
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत संजय ॥
sentences.tr:
dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre samavetāḥ yuyutsavaḥ |
māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāḥ ca eva kim akurvata saṃjaya ||

morph.gloss: sacred duty, the right order (here: 'of dharma', first member of the compound)
the Kuru clan, ancestors of both sides
field (loc. sg.: 'on the field of the Kurus')
assembled, gathered (past participle of sam-ava-i; nom. pl. masc.; final -ḥ dropped before the following y-)
wanting to fight (desiderative adjective from yudh 'fight'; nom. pl. masc.)
son of Pāṇḍu, a Pāṇḍava (nom. pl.; -āḥ + c- becomes -āś c-)
indeed, just (ca + eva fuse to caiva)
to do (akurvata: imperfect middle, 3rd pl. 'they did')
Sañjaya, the blind king's minister and narrator (vocative)

sentences.l: On the field of dharma, on the field of the Kurus, assembled, wanting-to-fight — my people and the sons of Pāṇḍu too — what did they do, Sañjaya?
sentences.i: On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered and eager for battle, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, Sañjaya?
sentences.n: The whole poem is framed as a report: the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks his minister Sañjaya, who has been granted sight of the distant battlefield, and everything that follows is Sañjaya's answer. Two things to notice on the first line. First, sandhi: पाण्डवाश्चैव looks like one word but is three — pāṇḍavāḥ + ca + eva, the final -ḥ turning to -ś before c-, and ca + eva fusing to caiva. You will see this fusing on nearly every line; the reading under each word shows the words unfused. Second, the opening compound dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre: Kurukṣetra is a real place north of Delhi, and the poet sets 'field of dharma' beside it — the battle is over what is right. Māmakāḥ, 'mine', is the king's word for his own hundred sons.

sentences.t: सञ्जय उवाच
sentences.tr: sañjaya uvāca
sentences.l: Sañjaya said

morph.gloss: Sañjaya, the king's minister and charioteer, who reports the battle to him (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा ।
आचार्यमुपसंगम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत् ॥
sentences.tr:
dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍava-anīkam vyūḍham duryodhanaḥ tadā |
ācāryam upasaṃgamya rājā vacanam abravīt ||

morph.gloss: army, battle-array (acc. sg.; -a + a- fuse to -ā-)
drawn up in battle order (past participle of vi-ūh; acc. sg. neut.)
the eldest Kaurava, leader of the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (nom. sg.; -aḥ + t- becomes -as t-)
teacher (acc. sg.; here Droṇa, who trained both families)
to approach (upasaṃgamya: gerund, 'having gone up to')

sentences.l: Having seen, then, the Pāṇḍava-army drawn-up, Duryodhana then, the teacher having-approached, the king spoke a word.
sentences.i: When he saw the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in battle order, King Duryodhana went up to his teacher and spoke.
sentences.n: Sanskrit narrative runs on gerunds — dṛṣṭvā 'having seen', upasaṃgamya 'having approached' — chained before a single finite verb, abravīt 'he spoke'. Read them as 'he saw ..., went up ..., and spoke'. The teacher is Droṇa, who taught the princes of both houses to fight. Vyūḍha, 'arrayed', is the technical word for an army in formation.

sentences.t:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम् ।
व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता ॥
sentences.tr:
paśya etām pāṇḍu-putrāṇām ācārya mahatīm camūm |
vyūḍhām drupada-putreṇa tava śiṣyeṇa dhīmatā ||

morph.gloss: this (etām: acc. sg. fem.; -a + e- fuse to -ai-)
Pāṇḍu, father of the five Pāṇḍavas
son (gen. pl. 'of the sons of Pāṇḍu')
son (instr. sg. 'by the son of Drupada', i.e. Dhṛṣṭadyumna)

sentences.l: Behold this of-the-sons-of-Pāṇḍu, O teacher, great army, drawn-up by the son of Drupada, by your pupil, the wise one.
sentences.i: 'Look, teacher, at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up by Drupada's son, your own clever pupil.'
sentences.n: Paśyaitām is paśya + etām: the imperative 'look!' fused with 'this'. The jab is in the last line: Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who arrayed the enemy, was Droṇa's pupil — and Drupada, his father, was Droṇa's old enemy. Duryodhana is needling his teacher. Note the four words that agree with camūm 'army' (feminine accusative): etām, mahatīm, vyūḍhām — Sanskrit lets them scatter across the verse, and the endings tie them together.

sentences.t:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि ।
युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः ॥
sentences.tr:
atra śūrāḥ mahā-iṣvāsāḥ bhīma-arjuna-samāḥ yudhi |
yuyudhānaḥ virāṭaḥ ca drupadaḥ ca mahā-rathaḥ ||

morph.gloss: bow, lit. 'arrow-thrower'; also 'archer' (nom. pl.: 'great bowmen'; -ā + i- fuse to -e-)
Bhīma, second Pāṇḍava, the strong one
equal (nom. pl.: 'equal to Bhīma and Arjuna')
Yuyudhāna, i.e. Sātyaki, a Vṛṣṇi warrior (nom. sg.; -aḥ before v- becomes -o)
Virāṭa, king of the Matsyas, who sheltered the Pāṇḍavas in exile
chariot; mahāratha 'great chariot-warrior', a champion who can fight ten thousand (nom. sg.)

sentences.l: Here are heroes, great-bowmen, to Bhīma and Arjuna equal in battle: Yuyudhāna and Virāṭa and Drupada the great-chariot-warrior.
sentences.i: 'Here are heroes, mighty archers, a match for Bhīma and Arjuna in battle: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada the great warrior.
sentences.n: The muster roll begins. Sanskrit strings names with ca ... ca, 'and ... and', where English uses one 'and'. Maheṣvāsa is mahā + iṣvāsa, 'great bow' used for the man who draws it. Mahāratha, literally 'great chariot', is a rank: a warrior able to fight ten thousand at once. The reading shows sandhi across the join: mahā + iṣvāsa gives maheṣvāsa, ā + i fusing to e.

sentences.t:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान् ।
पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः ॥
sentences.tr:
dhṛṣṭaketuḥ cekitānaḥ kāśi-rājaḥ ca vīryavān |
purujit kuntibhojaḥ ca śaibyaḥ ca nara-puṅgavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: king (kāśirāja: 'the king of Kāśī', nom. sg.)
Kuntibhoja, adoptive father of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍavas' mother
bull; 'bull among men', a champion (nom. sg.)

sentences.l: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the king of Kāśī the valorous; Purujit and Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, bull-among-men.
sentences.i: 'Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna and the valiant king of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, a bull among men.
sentences.n: A verse of names, which is what the whole first half of this chapter is. Narapuṅgava, 'man-bull', is a standing compliment: the bull is the best of the herd. Vīryavān, 'possessing vīrya' (manly force), is the -vat suffix you will meet constantly — 'having X'.

sentences.t:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान् ।
सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः ॥
sentences.tr:
yudhāmanyuḥ ca vikrāntaḥ uttamaujāḥ ca vīryavān |
saubhadraḥ draupadeyāḥ ca sarve eva mahā-rathāḥ ||

morph.gloss: valiant, bold (nom. sg.; final -aḥ dropped before the vowel u-)
Uttamaujas, a Pāñcāla prince, brother of Yudhāmanyu
'son of Subhadrā', i.e. Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son (nom. sg.; -aḥ before d- becomes -o)
'son of Draupadī': the five sons of the Pāṇḍavas by their shared wife (nom. pl.)
all (nom. pl.; final -e stays before a vowel)

sentences.l: Yudhāmanyu the valiant, and Uttamaujas the valorous; the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī, all indeed great-chariot-warriors.
sentences.i: 'Bold Yudhāmanyu, valiant Uttamaujas, Subhadrā's son and the sons of Draupadī — every one of them a great warrior.
sentences.n: Names formed from mothers: Saubhadra 'son of Subhadrā' is Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son; the Draupadeyas are the five sons of Draupadī, one by each of the five Pāṇḍava brothers, to whom she was jointly married. Vikrānta uttamaujāḥ: the final -ḥ of vikrāntaḥ simply drops before the vowel u-, so the written form is विक्रान्त with no visarga.

sentences.t:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम ।
नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते ॥
sentences.tr:
asmākam tu viśiṣṭāḥ ye tān nibodha dvija-uttama |
nāyakāḥ mama sainyasya saṃjñā-artham tān bravīmi te ||

morph.gloss: distinguished, outstanding (nom. pl.; -āḥ before y- becomes -ā)
to take note of (nibodha: imperative 2nd sg. 'take note!'; -n + n- written doubled)
best (vocative: 'O best of brahmins', addressed to Droṇa; -a + u- fuse to -o-)
purpose; saṃjñārtham 'for your information' (adverbial acc.; -ā + a- fuse to -ā-)

sentences.l: But of ours the distinguished ones, who [they are], take-note, O best of the twice-born; the leaders of my army, for information I name them to you.
sentences.i: 'But now take note, best of brahmins, of the outstanding men on our side, the leaders of my army; I name them so that you know them.
sentences.n: Dvijottama, 'best of the twice-born', addresses Droṇa as a brahmin — a brahmin who fights, which the poem does not remark on but the tradition did. The verse is built on a relative pair: ye ... tān, 'who ... them': 'those who are distinguished, take note of them'. Saṃjñārtham is an adverbial accusative, 'for the purpose of recognition'.

sentences.t:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिंजयः ।
अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च ॥
sentences.tr:
bhavān bhīṣmaḥ ca karṇaḥ ca kṛpaḥ ca samitiṃ-jayaḥ |
aśvatthāmā vikarṇaḥ ca saumadattiḥ tathā eva ca ||

morph.gloss: your honour, you (respectful 3rd-person form; nom. sg. bhavān)
Bhīṣma, grand-uncle of both sides and commander of the Kaurava army
Karṇa, Kuntī's secret first-born, fighting for the Kauravas
Kṛpa, a brahmin warrior and teacher
'son of Somadatta', i.e. Bhūriśravas (nom. sg.; -iḥ + t- becomes -is t-)

sentences.l: Your honour, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa, and Kṛpa victorious-in-battle; Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa and the son of Somadatta likewise.
sentences.i: 'Yourself, and Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa who always wins his fights; Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and Somadatta's son too.
sentences.n: Bhavān is the polite 'you' — grammatically third person ('your honour'), so it takes a third-person verb. Karṇa is the tragic figure of the epic: Kuntī's first son, born before her marriage and abandoned, so the Pāṇḍavas' elder brother without their knowing it. The text here follows the usual (Śaṅkara) reading saumadattis tathaiva ca; some editions, including the GRETIL e-text collated for this file, read saumadattir jayadrathaḥ, 'Saumadatti and Jayadratha', instead.

sentences.t:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः ।
नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः ॥
sentences.tr:
anye ca bahavaḥ śūrāḥ mad-arthe tyakta-jīvitāḥ |
nānā-śastra-praharaṇāḥ sarve yuddha-viśāradāḥ ||

morph.gloss: me, my (stem form of aham in compounds)
life (nom. pl.: 'having given up their lives', i.e. ready to die)
striking, means of attack (nom. pl.: 'striking with many kinds of weapon')

sentences.l: And other many heroes, for my sake having-given-up-their-lives, with-various-weapons-striking, all in-battle-skilled.
sentences.i: 'And many other heroes ready to lay down their lives for me, armed with weapons of every kind, all of them expert in war.
sentences.n: Three long compounds, each an adjective describing the heroes: tyakta-jīvitāḥ 'whose lives are given up' (a bahuvrīhi, the 'having-X' type of compound), nānā-śastra-praharaṇāḥ 'having various weapons as their means of striking', yuddha-viśāradāḥ 'battle-skilled'. Reading a Sanskrit compound means finding its last member (the head) and reading backwards.

sentences.t:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम् ।
पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम् ॥
sentences.tr:
aparyāptam tad asmākam balam bhīṣma-abhirakṣitam |
paryāptam tu idam eteṣām balam bhīma-abhirakṣitam ||

morph.gloss: insufficient; or 'unlimited' — see note (nom. sg. neut.)
to guard (abhirakṣita: past participle 'guarded'; nom. sg. neut.; -a + a- fuse to -ā-)
to guard (abhirakṣita: past participle; nom. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: Insufficient is that army of ours, by Bhīṣma guarded; sufficient however is this army of theirs, by Bhīma guarded.
sentences.i: 'Our army, with Bhīṣma at its head, is not enough; theirs, with Bhīma at its head, is enough.
sentences.n: A famous ambiguity. Aparyāpta means 'not sufficient', and paryāpta 'sufficient' — read that way, Duryodhana is confessing weakness. But aparyāpta can also mean 'unlimited' and paryāpta 'limited', which gives the boast most commentators prefer: 'our army is unlimited, theirs is limited'. The verse pairs Bhīṣma and Bhīma, the two great champions, in matching half-lines, and the poem itself does not settle which reading is right; the literal layer above gives the plain dictionary sense.

sentences.t:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः ।
भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि ॥
sentences.tr:
ayaneṣu ca sarveṣu yathā-bhāgam avasthitāḥ |
bhīṣmam eva abhirakṣantu bhavantaḥ sarve eva hi ||

morph.gloss: path, position, gap in the line (loc. pl.)
share, allotted place (yathābhāgam: adverbial 'each at his post')
to stand, take position (avasthita: past participle, nom. pl.)
to guard (abhirakṣantu: imperative 3rd pl. 'let them guard'; eva + a- fuse to evā-)

sentences.l: And in all the positions, each-at-his-post standing, Bhīṣma alone let-them-guard, your honours, all indeed.
sentences.i: 'So let all of you, each holding his own post in every part of the line, guard Bhīṣma above all.'
sentences.n: Bhīṣmam evābhirakṣantu: eva 'alone, above all' is the stress-word of the verse, and eva + abhirakṣantu fuse to evābhirakṣantu. Abhirakṣantu is a third-person imperative, 'let them guard'; with bhavantaḥ ('your honours', the polite plural) it works as a courteous command. Ayana is literally a 'going', here the gaps or stations of the battle-line.

sentences.t:
तस्य संजनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः ।
सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान् ॥
sentences.tr:
tasya saṃjanayan harṣam kuru-vṛddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ |
siṃha-nādam vinadya uccaiḥ śaṅkham dadhmau pratāpavān ||

morph.gloss: to produce (saṃjanayan: causative present participle, nom. sg. 'producing')
elder; 'the elder of the Kurus' (nom. sg.)
grandfather (nom. sg.; Bhīṣma, the grand-uncle counted as grandsire)
conch shell, blown as a war-trumpet (acc. sg.)

sentences.l: Of him producing joy, the Kuru-elder, the grandsire, a lion-roar having-roared aloud, a conch blew, the majestic one.
sentences.i: Then the grandsire, the old man of the Kurus, to cheer Duryodhana, roared like a lion and blew his conch.
sentences.n: Tasya harṣaṃ saṃjanayan, 'producing joy of him', i.e. to hearten Duryodhana, whom the speech has just betrayed as anxious. The grandsire is Bhīṣma, called pitāmaha 'grandfather' though strictly a grand-uncle. The conch (śaṅkha) is the war-trumpet of the epic; the next verses are a catalogue of them. Dadhmau is the perfect of dhmā 'to blow' — reduplicated, like Greek or Latin perfects.

sentences.t:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः ।
सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत् ॥
sentences.tr:
tataḥ śaṅkhāḥ ca bheryaḥ ca paṇava-ānaka-gomukhāḥ |
sahasā eva abhyahanyanta saḥ śabdaḥ tumulaḥ abhavat ||

morph.gloss: 'cow-mouth', a horn (nom. pl.; -a + ā- fuse to -ā-)
to strike, sound (abhyahanyanta: imperfect passive 3rd pl. 'were sounded'; sahasā + eva → sahasaiva; eva + a- → evā-)
that (saḥ: nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ dropped before a consonant)
tumultuous (nom. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o ' with the avagraha ऽ marking the lost a)

sentences.l: Then conches and kettledrums and tabors, drums and horns suddenly were sounded; that sound tumultuous was.
sentences.i: Then conches, kettledrums, tabors, big drums and horns all at once were sounded, and the noise was tremendous.
sentences.n: The last three words are a sandhi exercise: śabdastumulo'bhavat is śabdaḥ + tumulaḥ + abhavat. The first -aḥ becomes -as before t-; the second becomes -o before a-, and the a- of abhavat then vanishes, its absence marked in Devanagari by the sign ऽ (avagraha), which the transliteration shows as an apostrophe. Abhyahanyanta is a passive, 'were struck': drums are 'struck' even when they are blown.

sentences.t:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ ।
माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः ॥
sentences.tr:
tataḥ śvetaiḥ hayaiḥ yukte mahati syandane sthitau |
mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaḥ ca eva divyau śaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ ||

morph.gloss: yoked (loc. sg.: 'yoked with white horses'; -aiḥ + h-/y- → -air)
son of Pāṇḍu, here Arjuna (nom. sg.)
to blow (pradadhmatuḥ: perfect 3rd dual 'the two blew')

sentences.l: Then, with white horses yoked, in a great chariot standing, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava too their divine conches blew, the two.
sentences.i: Then, standing in a great chariot yoked with white horses, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna blew their divine conches.
sentences.n: Sanskrit has a dual number for exactly two: sthitau 'the two standing', divyau śaṅkhau 'the two divine conches', pradadhmatuḥ 'the two blew'. Mādhava (descendant of Madhu) is Kṛṣṇa; 'the Pāṇḍava' here is Arjuna, whose chariot Kṛṣṇa drives. Note the locative absolute: śvetair hayair yukte ... syandane sthitau, 'standing in a chariot yoked with white horses'.

sentences.t:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनञ्जयः ।
पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः ॥
sentences.tr:
pāñcajanyam hṛṣīkeśaḥ devadattam dhanañjayaḥ |
pauṇḍram dadhmau mahā-śaṅkham bhīma-karmā vṛka-udaraḥ ||

morph.gloss: Pāñcajanya, Kṛṣṇa's conch, taken from the demon Pañcajana (acc. sg.)
'lord of the senses', Kṛṣṇa (nom. sg.; -aḥ before d- → -o)
belly; Vṛkodara 'wolf-belly', Bhīma's nickname for his appetite (nom. sg.; -a + u- → -o-)

sentences.l: Pāñcajanya the Lord-of-the-senses, Devadatta the Winner-of-wealth; Pauṇḍra blew, the great conch, the one-of-terrible-deeds, Wolf-belly.
sentences.i: Kṛṣṇa blew Pāñcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of the terrible deeds, the Wolf-belly, blew his great conch Pauṇḍra.
sentences.n: Every name here is an epithet, and the poem uses them the way Homer uses 'swift-footed': Hṛṣīkeśa 'lord of the senses' is Kṛṣṇa, Dhanañjaya 'winner of wealth' is Arjuna, Vṛkodara 'wolf-belly' is Bhīma, famous for his appetite. The one verb dadhmau serves all three clauses. The conches have names too, as swords do in Beowulf.

sentences.t:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः ।
नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ ॥
sentences.tr:
ananta-vijayam rājā kuntī-putraḥ yudhiṣṭhiraḥ |
nakulaḥ sahadevaḥ ca sughoṣa-maṇipuṣpakau ||

morph.gloss: Kuntī, mother of the three elder Pāṇḍavas
Yudhiṣṭhira, the eldest Pāṇḍava, 'steady in battle' (nom. sg.)
Nakula, fourth Pāṇḍava, twin of Sahadeva (nom. sg.)
'jewel-flowered', Sahadeva's conch (acc. dual: the two conches)

sentences.l: Anantavijaya the king, Kuntī's-son Yudhiṣṭhira; Nakula and Sahadeva Sughoṣa-and-Maṇipuṣpaka.
sentences.i: King Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī's son, blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
sentences.n: The verb is carried over from verse 15 — no verb appears here at all. Sughoṣa-maṇipuṣpakau is a dvandva, a pair-compound, in the dual: 'Sughoṣa-and-Maṇipuṣpaka', one conch each for the twins. Yudhiṣṭhira is 'the king' (rājā) because he is the eldest Pāṇḍava and the rightful heir.

sentences.t:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः ।
धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः ॥
sentences.tr:
kāśyaḥ ca parama-iṣvāsaḥ śikhaṇḍī ca mahā-rathaḥ |
dhṛṣṭadyumnaḥ virāṭaḥ ca sātyakiḥ ca aparājitaḥ ||

morph.gloss: Śikhaṇḍin, Drupada's child, born a girl and become a man, fated to bring Bhīṣma down (nom. sg.)
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, son of Drupada, commander of the Pāṇḍava army (nom. sg.; -aḥ before v- → -o)
Sātyaki (= Yuyudhāna of verse 4), Kṛṣṇa's kinsman

sentences.l: And the Kāśī-king, supreme-archer, and Śikhaṇḍin the great-chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa and Sātyaki the unconquered,
sentences.i: And the king of Kāśī, a supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin the great warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki the unconquered,
sentences.n: Verses 17 and 18 are one sentence; the verb comes at the end of 18. Śikhaṇḍin has the strangest story on the field: born a daughter of Drupada, raised as a son, and later made male by a spirit's gift — Bhīṣma will refuse to fight him, and that refusal is how Bhīṣma falls. Sātyaki is the same man as Yuyudhāna in verse 4.

sentences.t:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते ।
सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक् ॥
sentences.tr:
drupadaḥ draupadeyāḥ ca sarvaśaḥ pṛthivī-pate |
saubhadraḥ ca mahā-bāhuḥ śaṅkhān dadhmuḥ pṛthak pṛthak ||

morph.gloss: lord; pṛthivīpati 'lord of the earth' (vocative, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra)

sentences.l: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī all-together, O lord of the earth, and the son of Subhadrā the mighty-armed — the conches they blew, each-his-own.
sentences.i: and Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and Subhadrā's mighty-armed son, each blew his own conch.
sentences.n: Pṛthivīpate, 'lord of the earth', is Sañjaya addressing the blind king — a reminder that all of this is being reported to him. Pṛthak pṛthak, 'separately, separately', is the Sanskrit way of saying 'each his own'; doubling a word for distribution is common. Dadhmuḥ is the plural of the perfect: 'they blew'.

sentences.t:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत् ।
नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलो व्यनुनादयन् ॥
sentences.tr:
saḥ ghoṣaḥ dhārtarāṣṭrāṇām hṛdayāni vyadārayat |
nabhaḥ ca pṛthivīm ca eva tumulaḥ vyanunādayan ||

morph.gloss: son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a Kaurava (gen. pl.)
to tear apart (vyadārayat: causative imperfect 3rd sg. 'it rent')
to make resound (vyanunādayan: causative present participle, nom. sg. 'making resound')

sentences.l: That din of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra the hearts tore-apart, sky and earth too, tumultuous, making-resound.
sentences.i: That din, resounding through sky and earth, tore the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.
sentences.n: Dhārtarāṣṭra, 'son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra', is the poem's word for the Kaurava side, and the king hearing this is Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself. Vyadārayat is a causative, 'caused to split'; vyanunādayan, a causative participle, 'making [sky and earth] resound' — the -aya- in each is the causative mark. Nabhaś ca: nabhaḥ + ca, the visarga turning to ś before c.

sentences.t:
अथ व्यवस्थितान्दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान्कपिध्वजः ।
प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसंपाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः ॥
sentences.tr:
atha vyavasthitān dṛṣṭvā dhārtarāṣṭrān kapi-dhvajaḥ |
pravṛtte śastra-saṃpāte dhanuḥ udyamya pāṇḍavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to be arrayed, take up position (vyavasthita: past participle, acc. pl.)
banner; Kapidhvaja 'monkey-bannered', Arjuna, whose flag bears Hanumān (nom. sg.)
to begin (pravṛtta: past participle, loc. sg.: 'as ... was beginning')
clash, flying-together (loc. sg.: locative absolute with pravṛtte)
son of Pāṇḍu, here Arjuna (nom. sg.)

sentences.l: Then, arrayed having-seen the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Monkey-bannered one, as the weapon-clash was beginning, his bow having-raised, the Pāṇḍava
sentences.i: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up for battle, and the clash of weapons about to begin, Arjuna of the monkey banner raised his bow
sentences.n: Verses 20 and 21 are one sentence: the subject 'the Pāṇḍava' (Arjuna) is introduced here and does his speaking in the next verse. Kapidhvaja, 'monkey-bannered': the monkey-god Hanumān sits on Arjuna's flag. Pravṛtte śastrasaṃpāte is a locative absolute, 'the weapon-clash having begun' — the absolute construction, two locatives together, serves as a whole clause of time.

sentences.t: अर्जुन उवाच
sentences.tr: arjuna uvāca
sentences.l: Arjuna said

morph.gloss: Arjuna, the third Pāṇḍava, the great archer (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत ॥
sentences.tr:
hṛṣīkeśam tadā vākyam idam āha mahī-pate |
senayoḥ ubhayoḥ madhye ratham sthāpaya me acyuta ||

morph.gloss: lord; mahīpati 'lord of the earth' (vocative, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra)
to stand (sthāpaya: causative imperative 2nd sg. 'make stand, halt!')

sentences.l: to the Lord-of-the-senses then this word said, O lord of the earth: 'Between the two armies, in the middle, my chariot halt, O Unshakeable one.
sentences.i: and said this to Kṛṣṇa, O lord of the earth: 'Halt my chariot between the two armies, Acyuta,
sentences.n: The finite verb of verses 20–21 is āha, 'he said'. Senayor ubhayor madhye — 'in the middle of both armies' — is repeated word for word in verse 24, when Kṛṣṇa does it. Sthāpaya is the causative imperative of sthā 'stand': 'make [it] stand', i.e. halt. Me 'cyuta: me + acyuta, with the avagraha marking the swallowed a-.

sentences.t:
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान् ।
कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन् रणसमुद्यमे ॥
sentences.tr:
yāvat etān nirīkṣe aham yoddhu-kāmān avasthitān |
kaiḥ mayā saha yoddhavyam asmin raṇa-samudyame ||

morph.gloss: as long as, until (yāvad before a vowel)
to look at, survey (nirīkṣe: present middle 1st sg. 'I survey')
to fight (yoddhu-: infinitive stem in compound)
to take position (avasthita: past participle, acc. pl. 'arrayed')
who? (kaiḥ: instr. pl. 'with whom'; -aiḥ + m- → -air m-)
to fight (yoddhavya: gerundive 'is to be fought', nom. sg. neut.: impersonal 'fighting must be done')

sentences.l: until I survey these, wanting-to-fight, standing-arrayed — with whom by me together it-must-be-fought in this battle-enterprise.
sentences.i: so that I can look over these men standing here eager for battle, and see whom I must fight in this great undertaking.
sentences.n: Yoddhavyam is a gerundive, 'is to be fought', used impersonally: 'fighting must be done by me' (mayā) 'together with whom' (kaiḥ saha) — the Sanskrit passive-impersonal where English says 'whom I must fight'. Nirīkṣe is a middle-voice form, 'I look over for myself'. The Wikisource text prints निरिक्षे with a short i, a misprint; the verb is nir-īkṣ with long ī, as in the GRETIL text, and the long vowel is printed here.

sentences.t:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः ॥
sentences.tr:
yotsyamānān avekṣe aham ye ete atra samāgatāḥ |
dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheḥ yuddhe priya-cikīrṣavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to fight (yotsyamāna: future participle middle, acc. pl. 'those about to fight')
to look at (avekṣe: present middle 1st sg. 'I look at')
who (ye: nom. pl. masc. relative; final -e stays before a vowel)
to come together (samāgata: past participle, nom. pl. 'assembled')
the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, i.e. Duryodhana (gen. sg.)
evil-minded (gen. sg., agreeing with dhārtarāṣṭrasya; -eḥ + y- → -er y-)
wishing to do (desiderative adjective from kṛ; nom. pl.: 'wishing to do a favour to')

sentences.l: Those-about-to-fight I look-at, who these here are-assembled, of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, the evil-minded, in battle wishing-to-do-a-favour.'
sentences.i: Let me see who has come here to fight, eager to please the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.'
sentences.n: Ya ete 'tra: the relative ye 'who' loses its final -e's independence before a vowel and is written य; ete + atra gives ete 'tra with avagraha. Dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheḥ, 'of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra', is Duryodhana in the singular. Priyacikīrṣavaḥ is a desiderative adjective — cikīrṣu 'wishing to do', from kṛ — the same formation as yuyutsu 'wishing to fight' in verse 1.

sentences.t: सञ्जय उवाच
sentences.tr: sañjaya uvāca
sentences.l: Sañjaya said

morph.gloss: Sañjaya, the king's minister and charioteer, who reports the battle to him (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम् ॥
sentences.tr:
evam uktaḥ hṛṣīkeśaḥ guḍākeśena bhārata |
senayoḥ ubhayoḥ madhye sthāpayitvā ratha-uttamam ||

morph.gloss: to speak (ukta: past participle 'addressed', nom. sg.; -aḥ before h- → -o)
'thick-haired' or 'conqueror of sleep', Arjuna (instr. sg. 'by Guḍākeśa')
best (rathottama: 'the best of chariots', acc. sg.; -a + u- → -o-)

sentences.l: Thus addressed, the Lord-of-the-senses by the Thick-haired one, O Bhārata, between the two armies in the middle having-halted the best-of-chariots,
sentences.i: Addressed in this way by Arjuna, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa halted that finest of chariots between the two armies,
sentences.n: Guḍākeśa, an epithet of Arjuna, is explained two ways by the tradition: 'thick-haired' or 'conqueror of sleep' (guḍākā). Bhārata, 'descendant of Bharata', is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the same title is later given to Arjuna, since both houses descend from Bharata. Verses 24–25 are one sentence, ending in uvāca 'he said'.

sentences.t:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम् ।
उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति ॥
sentences.tr:
bhīṣma-droṇa-pramukhataḥ sarveṣām ca mahī-kṣitām |
uvāca pārtha paśya etān samavetān kurūn iti ||

morph.gloss: in front of, facing (adverb with the compound: 'in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa')
ruler (mahīkṣit 'ruler of the earth', gen. pl. 'of all the kings')
the Kurus (acc. pl. kurūn: here both sides, all descendants of Kuru)

sentences.l: in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and of all the rulers-of-the-earth, said: 'O son of Pṛthā, behold these assembled Kurus' — thus.
sentences.i: facing Bhīṣma, Droṇa and all the kings, and said: 'Arjuna, behold these Kurus gathered here.'
sentences.n: Iti at the end marks the close of a quotation — Sanskrit's closing quotation mark, placed after the words spoken. Note that Kṛṣṇa says kurūn, 'Kurus': both armies are Kurus, descendants of Kuru, and the word quietly makes Arjuna's point for him before he makes it. Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā' (another name of Kuntī), is Kṛṣṇa's usual address to Arjuna.

sentences.t:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितॄनथ पितामहान् ।
आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातॄन्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा ॥
sentences.tr:
tatra apaśyat sthitān pārthaḥ pitṝn atha pitāmahān |
ācāryān mātulān bhrātṝn putrān pautrān sakhīn tathā ||

morph.gloss: to see (apaśyat: imperfect 3rd sg. 'he saw'; tatra + a- → tatrā-)
father (pitṝn: acc. pl. 'fathers', i.e. paternal uncles and elders)

words.reading: ācāryān mātulān bhrātṝn putrān pautrān sakhīn tathā

glyphs.tr: ācāryān mātulān bhrātṝn putrān pautrān sakhīn tathā

morph.gloss: friend, companion (sakhīn: acc. pl.; -n + t- → -ṃs t-)

sentences.l: There saw, standing, the son of Pṛthā fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal-uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends likewise,
sentences.i: There Arjuna saw, standing in their ranks, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends,
sentences.n: The second line is one unbroken Devanagari string — ācāryānmātulānbhrātṝnputrānpautrānsakhīṃstathā — because each accusative plural ends in a consonant (-n) and Sanskrit writes a consonant-final word joined to the next. The reading under it separates the seven words. Pitṝn 'fathers' means the father's generation — uncles like Bhīṣma's kin, not Arjuna's own father Pāṇḍu, who is dead. Sakhīṃs tathā: the final -n of sakhīn becomes -ṃs before t-.

sentences.t:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि ।
तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान् ॥
sentences.tr:
śvaśurān suhṛdaḥ ca eva senayoḥ ubhayoḥ api |
tān samīkṣya saḥ kaunteyaḥ sarvān bandhūn avasthitān ||
sentences.l: fathers-in-law and friends too, in both the armies alike. Them having-surveyed, he, Kuntī's son, all the kinsmen standing-arrayed,
sentences.i: fathers-in-law and friends as well, in both armies alike. When Kuntī's son had looked over all those kinsmen standing there,
sentences.n: Ubhayor api — 'in both, even': the point of the whole list is that the same kinds of kin stand on both sides. Verses 27–28 form one sentence: the gerund samīkṣya 'having surveyed' here, the finite verb abravīt 'he spoke' in the next verse. Kaunteya 'son of Kuntī' is a third way of naming Arjuna by his mother (with Pārtha).

sentences.t: अर्जुन उवाच
sentences.tr: arjuna uvāca
sentences.l: Arjuna said

morph.gloss: Arjuna, the third Pāṇḍava, the great archer (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
कृपया परयाविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत् ।
दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम् ॥
sentences.tr:
kṛpayā parayā āviṣṭaḥ viṣīdan idam abravīt |
dṛṣṭvā imam sva-janam kṛṣṇa yuyutsum samupasthitam ||

morph.gloss: supreme, deep (parayā: instr. sg. fem., with kṛpayā)
to enter (āviṣṭa: past participle 'entered into, overcome'; nom. sg.; -ā + ā- → -ā-; -aḥ before v- → -o)
to sink, despair (viṣīdan: present participle, nom. sg. 'despairing'; -n + i- written -nn-)
people; svajana 'kinsfolk, one's own people' (acc. sg.)
to stand near, be present (samupasthita: past participle, acc. sg. 'drawn up')

sentences.l: by pity supreme overcome, despairing, this he spoke: 'Having seen this own-people, Kṛṣṇa, wanting-to-fight, drawn-up,
sentences.i: he was overcome by deep pity and said in despair: 'Krishna, seeing my own people here, drawn up and eager for battle,
sentences.n: Kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ: 'entered by supreme pity' — āviṣṭa, from ā-viś 'enter', is the word for being possessed, as by a spirit; the emotion takes Arjuna over. Viṣīdan 'sinking, despairing' gives the chapter its traditional title, Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga, 'the yoga of Arjuna's despair'. Svajana, 'own-people', is the key word of the chapter: not 'the enemy' but 'my own'.

sentences.t:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति ।
वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते ॥
sentences.tr:
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukham ca pariśuṣyati |
vepathuḥ ca śarīre me roma-harṣaḥ ca jāyate ||

morph.gloss: to sink, give way (sīdanti: present 3rd pl.)
bristling; romaharṣa 'the hair standing on end' (nom. sg.)
to be born, arise (jāyate: present middle 3rd sg. 'arises')

sentences.l: sink my limbs, and the mouth dries-up, and trembling in my body and hair-bristling arises.
sentences.i: my limbs give way, my mouth goes dry, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
sentences.n: The symptoms of shock, listed with present-tense verbs: sīdanti 'they sink', pariśuṣyati 'it dries up', jāyate 'it arises'. Mama and me are both 'my' — mama the full form, me the short enclitic that cannot stand first in a clause. Romaharṣa, 'hair-thrill', is horripilation, the hair standing on end; in Sanskrit poetry it can be a sign of joy as easily as of dread.

sentences.t:
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते ।
न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः ॥
sentences.tr:
gāṇḍīvam sraṃsate hastāt tvak ca eva paridahyate |
na ca śaknomi avasthātum bhramati iva ca me manaḥ ||

morph.gloss: Gāṇḍīva, Arjuna's great bow (nom. sg. neut.)
to slip, fall (sraṃsate: present middle 3rd sg. 'slips')
to burn all over (paridahyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is burning')
to be able (śaknomi: present 1st sg. 'I can'; -i + a- → -y a-)

sentences.l: Gāṇḍīva slips from the hand, and the skin too burns-all-over; and I cannot stand, and reels, as it were, my mind.
sentences.i: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, my skin is burning all over; I cannot stay on my feet, and my mind seems to reel.
sentences.n: Gāṇḍīva is Arjuna's bow, a named weapon like a sword in Beowulf. Śaknomy avasthātum: śaknomi 'I am able' + the infinitive; -i before a vowel becomes -y, which is why the written form is शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं. Bhramatīva is bhramati + iva, 'reels as it were' — iva, 'like, as if', is the poet's constant softener.

sentences.t:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव ।
न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे ॥
sentences.tr:
nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni keśava |
na ca śreyaḥ anupaśyāmi hatvā sva-janam āhave ||

morph.gloss: good, welfare, anything better (acc. sg. neut.; -aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha)

sentences.l: And I see omens contrary, O Keśava, and I do not foresee good, having killed own-people in battle.
sentences.i: I see evil omens, Keśava, and I can see no good coming from killing my own people in battle.
sentences.n: Śreyo 'nupaśyāmi: śreyaḥ + anupaśyāmi, -aḥ becoming -o before a- and the a- dropping (avagraha). Śreyas, 'the better thing, welfare', is one of the Gītā's central words; the next chapter turns on it. Hatvā, 'having killed', is the gerund of han — the same root gives hantum 'to kill' in verse 35 and ghnataḥ 'killing' in the same verse.

sentences.t:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च ।
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा ॥
sentences.tr:
na kāṅkṣe vijayam kṛṣṇa na ca rājyam sukhāni ca |
kim naḥ rājyena govinda kim bhogaiḥ jīvitena vā ||

morph.gloss: to desire (kāṅkṣe: present middle 1st sg. 'I desire')
I (naḥ: enclitic gen./dat. pl. 'to us'; -aḥ before r- → -o)

sentences.l: I do not desire victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom and pleasures. What to us with a kingdom, Govinda, what with enjoyments or with life?
sentences.i: I have no wish for victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor for a kingdom and its pleasures. What good is a kingdom to us, Govinda — what good are pleasures, or life itself?
sentences.n: Kiṃ naḥ rājyena — 'what [is there] to us by a kingdom?' — is the Sanskrit idiom for 'what use is a kingdom to us?': kim with a dative of the person and an instrumental of the thing. Govinda, 'finder of cows', recalls Kṛṣṇa's youth as a cowherd. The verse has four ca's and one vā ('or'); Sanskrit likes to mark each item.

sentences.t:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च ।
त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च ॥
sentences.tr:
yeṣām arthe kāṅkṣitam naḥ rājyam bhogāḥ sukhāni ca |
te ime avasthitāḥ yuddhe prāṇān tyaktvā dhanāni ca ||

morph.gloss: to desire (kāṅkṣita: past participle 'desired', nom. sg. neut.)
I (naḥ: enclitic gen. pl. 'by us, our')
they (te: nom. pl. masc.; final -e stays before a vowel)
arrayed, standing (nom. pl.; -e + a- → -e ' with avagraha; -āḥ before y- → -ā)

sentences.l: For whose sake is desired by us the kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures — they, these, stand-arrayed in battle, their lives having-given-up, and their wealth.
sentences.i: The very people for whose sake we wanted a kingdom, enjoyment and pleasure are standing here in battle, ready to give up their lives and their wealth.
sentences.n: Yeṣām ... te: the relative-correlative frame again, 'of whom ... they'. Kāṅkṣitam is a past participle used as the predicate, 'is desired', with the agent in the enclitic naḥ 'by us'. Ta ime 'vasthitāḥ: te loses the -e's independence before a vowel (written त), and ime + avasthitāḥ fuse with the avagraha.

sentences.t:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः ।
मातुलाः श्वशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः संबन्धिनस्तथा ॥
sentences.tr:
ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāḥ tathā eva ca pitāmahāḥ |
mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ saṃbandhinaḥ tathā ||

morph.gloss: father (nom. pl. 'fathers', i.e. elders of the father's generation)
relative by marriage, kinsman (nom. pl.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)

sentences.l: Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, maternal-uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and kinsmen likewise.
sentences.i: Teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers, uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and kinsmen —
sentences.n: The same kin-list as verse 26, now in the nominative, as the subject of the sentence that runs through verse 35: these are the ones Arjuna will not kill. Two words are new: śyāla 'wife's brother' and saṃbandhin 'relative by marriage'. Putrās tathaiva: putrāḥ + tathā + eva, with -āḥ becoming -ās before t-.

sentences.t:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन ।
अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते ॥
sentences.tr:
etān na hantum icchāmi ghnataḥ api madhusūdana |
api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ kim nu mahī-kṛte ||

morph.gloss: to kill (ghnataḥ: present participle, acc. pl. 'though they are killing [me]'; -aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha)
kingship (gen. sg.: 'of sovereignty over the three worlds')
cause, sake (gen. sg., with the preceding genitive: 'for the sake of')
for the sake of (postposition; mahīkṛte 'for the sake of the earth')

sentences.l: These I do not wish to kill, even though they are killing, O slayer of Madhu — even for the sake of the kingship of the three worlds; how much less for the sake of the earth!
sentences.i: I do not want to kill them, Madhusūdana, even if they kill me — not for the sake of ruling all three worlds, let alone for the sake of the earth.
sentences.n: Ghnato 'pi — 'even [them] killing', i.e. even if they are the ones doing the killing: a participle in the accusative agreeing with etān. Api ... kiṃ nu: 'even for X; how much less for Y' — a standard Sanskrit escalation. Trailokya is the triple world of Vedic cosmology (earth, air, heaven); Madhusūdana names Kṛṣṇa as the god who slew the demon Madhu.

sentences.t:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन ।
पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः ॥
sentences.tr:
nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāt janārdana |
pāpam eva āśrayet asmān hatvā etān ātatāyinaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to be (syāt: optative 3rd sg. 'would be'; -t + j- → -j j-)

words.reading: pāpam eva āśrayet asmān hatvā etān ātatāyinaḥ

glyphs.tr: pāpam eva āśrayet asmān hatvā etān ātatāyinaḥ

morph.gloss: to cling to, attach to (āśrayet: optative 3rd sg. 'would cling to'; eva + ā- → evā-)
one who comes with drawn bow, an aggressor, a felon (acc. pl.)

sentences.l: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, for us what joy would there be, O Janārdana? Evil alone would cling to us, having killed these aggressors.
sentences.i: What joy could we have, Janārdana, in killing Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons? Only sin would come to us if we killed them, aggressors though they are.
sentences.n: The second line is one unbroken string of eight words in the Devanagari — see the reading. Ātatāyin, 'one who comes with bow drawn', is a legal term: an aggressor whom the law-books allow one to kill without guilt. Arjuna grants the point (they are ātatāyinaḥ) and rejects the permission. Syāj janārdana: syāt + janārdana, -t assimilating to the following j-.

sentences.t:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान् ।
स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव ॥
sentences.tr:
tasmāt na arhāḥ vayam hantum dhārtarāṣṭrān sva-bāndhavān |
sva-janam hi katham hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava ||

morph.gloss: entitled, right (nom. pl. 'we are not entitled'; na + a- → nā-; -āḥ before v- → -ā)
to be (syāma: optative 1st pl. 'could we be')

sentences.l: Therefore we are not entitled to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen; for our own people having killed, how could we be happy, O Mādhava?
sentences.i: So it is not right for us to kill Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, our own relations. How could we be happy, Mādhava, after killing our own people?
sentences.n: Nārhāḥ is na + arhāḥ, 'not entitled, not right': arha with an infinitive (hantum) is how Sanskrit says 'ought to'. Syāma is the optative, 'we might be' — the mood of what could or should happen, which the whole speech is written in. Svabāndhavān and svajanam: the prefix sva- 'own' twice in one verse.

sentences.t:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yadi api ete na paśyanti lobha-upahata-cetasaḥ |
kula-kṣaya-kṛtam doṣam mitra-drohe ca pātakam ||

morph.gloss: mind (nom. pl. bahuvrīhi: 'their minds ruined by greed'; -a + u- → -o-)
done, caused (acc. sg.: 'caused by the ruin of the family')
crime, that which makes one fall (acc. sg.)

sentences.l: Even if these do not see, their-minds-ruined-by-greed, the fault caused-by-the-ruin-of-the-family and the crime in treachery-to-friends,
sentences.i: Even if these men, their judgement ruined by greed, cannot see the evil in destroying a family or the crime of betraying friends,
sentences.n: Yady apy ete is yadi + api + ete: two final -i's become -y before vowels. Lobhopahatacetasaḥ is a bahuvrīhi describing ete: 'whose minds (cetas) are struck (upahata) by greed (lobha)'. The verse is the 'if' half of a sentence completed in 39.

sentences.t:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम् ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन ॥
sentences.tr:
katham na jñeyam asmābhiḥ pāpāt asmāt nivartitum |
kula-kṣaya-kṛtam doṣam prapaśyadbhiḥ janārdana ||

morph.gloss: to know (jñeya: gerundive 'to be known', nom. sg. neut.: 'should it not be known')
to turn back (nivartitum: infinitive 'to turn back')
to see clearly (prapaśyat: present participle, instr. pl. 'by us who see clearly'; -iḥ + j- → -ir j-)

sentences.l: how should it not be known by us, from this evil to turn back — the fault caused-by-the-ruin-of-the-family clearly-seeing, O Janārdana?
sentences.i: how can we, who see clearly the evil in destroying a family, not know enough to turn back from this sin, Janārdana?
sentences.n: Jñeyam asmābhiḥ — 'to be known by us' — the gerundive again, as in verse 22, with the agent in the instrumental. Prapaśyadbhiḥ 'by [us] seeing clearly' agrees with asmābhiḥ. Pāpād asmān nivartitum: the ablative 'from this sin' with the infinitive 'to turn back'; note -t + a- → -d a- and -t + n- → -n n- in the written string.

sentences.t:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः ।
धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत ॥
sentences.tr:
kula-kṣaye praṇaśyanti kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ |
dharme naṣṭe kulam kṛtsnam adharmaḥ abhibhavati uta ||

morph.gloss: destruction (loc. sg.: 'when the family is destroyed')
law, custom, sacred duty (nom. pl. 'the family laws')
to perish (naṣṭa: past participle, loc. sg.: locative absolute 'when dharma has perished')
lawlessness, un-dharma (nom. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o ' with avagraha)
to overpower (abhibhavati: present 3rd sg.; -i + u- → -y u-)

sentences.l: In the ruin of the family perish the family-laws, the eternal ones; when the law has perished, the whole family lawlessness overpowers too.
sentences.i: When a family is destroyed, its age-old laws perish; and when the law is gone, lawlessness overwhelms the whole family.
sentences.n: Dharma here is the concrete kula-dharma, the customs and duties of a particular family, not an abstraction. Dharme naṣṭe is a locative absolute, 'the dharma being lost'. Kṛtsnam adharmo 'bhibhavaty uta: four words fused in the writing — adharmaḥ + abhibhavati gives adharmo 'bhi-, and -ti + uta gives -ty uta.

sentences.t:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः ।
स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसंकरः ॥
sentences.tr:
adharma-abhibhavāt kṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kula-striyaḥ |
strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṃkaraḥ ||

morph.gloss: overpowering, prevailing (abl. sg. 'from the prevailing of lawlessness'; -a + a- → -ā-)
woman (nom. pl. striyaḥ: 'the women of the family')
corrupted (loc. pl. fem.: locative absolute 'when the women are corrupted')
mixing, confusion (nom. sg.: 'confusion of the classes')

sentences.l: From the overpowering of lawlessness, Kṛṣṇa, are corrupted the women of the family; when the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, arises class-confusion.
sentences.i: When lawlessness prevails, Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, Vārṣṇeya, the classes become mixed.
sentences.n: Arjuna's argument now runs as a chain of causes, each verse taking the last word of the previous as its starting point (adharma → adharmābhibhavāt). Strīṣu duṣṭāsu is a locative absolute, 'the women being corrupted'. Varṇasaṃkara, 'mixing of the varṇas' (the four social classes), was the classical Indian nightmare of social collapse. Vārṣṇeya: Kṛṣṇa as a member of the Vṛṣṇi clan.

sentences.t:
संकरो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च ।
पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः ॥
sentences.tr:
saṃkaraḥ narakāya eva kula-ghnānām kulasya ca |
patanti pitaraḥ hi eṣām lupta-piṇḍa-udaka-kriyāḥ ||

morph.gloss: killer, destroyer (gen. pl.: 'of the destroyers of the family')
father (pitaraḥ: nom. pl. 'the ancestors'; -aḥ before h- → -o)
lost, cut off (past participle of lup)
rite (nom. pl. bahuvrīhi: 'their rites of rice-ball and water cut off'; -a + u- → -o-)

sentences.l: Confusion is for hell alone, of the family-destroyers and of the family; for fall their ancestors, their rice-ball-and-water-rites cut off.
sentences.i: That mixing leads straight to hell, both for the family's destroyers and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice and water.
sentences.n: The ancestors (pitaraḥ, the 'fathers') depend on their descendants' offerings: the piṇḍa, a ball of cooked rice, and udaka, water, offered at the śrāddha rite. Without living heirs of pure line to perform them, the dead 'fall' from their place. Luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ is a four-member bahuvrīhi: 'whose piṇḍa-and-water-rites are cut off'. Narakāyaiva: narakāya + eva.

sentences.t:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसंकरकारकैः ।
उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः ॥
sentences.tr:
doṣaiḥ etaiḥ kula-ghnānām varṇa-saṃkara-kārakaiḥ |
utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ kula-dharmāḥ ca śāśvatāḥ ||

morph.gloss: fault (instr. pl. 'by these faults'; -aiḥ + e- → -air e-)
causing (instr. pl.: 'which cause the confusion of the classes')
to abolish (utsādyante: causative passive 3rd pl. 'are abolished')

sentences.l: By these faults of the family-destroyers, which-cause-class-confusion, are abolished the caste-laws and the family-laws, the everlasting ones.
sentences.i: Through these sins of the family's destroyers, which throw the classes into confusion, the everlasting laws of caste and family are wiped out.
sentences.n: The whole first line is instrumental — 'by these faults ... of the destroyers ... causing confusion' — and the second line gives the passive verb and its subject: utsādyante 'are abolished', jātidharmāḥ kuladharmāś ca. Jāti, 'birth-group', is the narrower unit within the broad varṇa. Kuladharmāś ca: -āḥ + ca → -āś ca.

sentences.t:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन ।
नरकेऽनियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम ॥
sentences.tr:
utsanna-kula-dharmāṇām manuṣyāṇām janārdana |
narake aniyatam vāsaḥ bhavati iti anuśuśruma ||

morph.gloss: law (gen. pl. bahuvrīhi: 'of men whose family laws are destroyed')
indefinite, unending (adverbial acc. 'for an indefinite time'; -e + a- → -e ' with avagraha; see note for the variant niyatam)
thus (closes the reported statement; -i + a- → -y a-)
to hear by tradition (anuśuśruma: perfect 1st pl. 'we have heard')

sentences.l: Of men whose-family-laws-are-destroyed, O Janārdana, in hell for-an-indefinite-time a dwelling comes to be — thus we have heard.
sentences.i: Men whose family laws have been destroyed, Janārdana, must dwell in hell for an unending time — so we have heard it told.
sentences.n: Anuśuśruma, 'we have heard by tradition', is a perfect of śru 'hear' with anu-, the verb for received teaching; Arjuna is citing what he was taught, not his own view. The text follows the reading narake 'niyatam, 'in hell, for an indefinite time' (aniyatam), the reading Śaṅkara's commentary explains; many printed editions read narake niyatam, 'in hell, certainly', which the GRETIL e-text also has. Bhavatīty anuśuśruma: bhavati + iti + anuśuśruma, with -i + i- → -ī- and -i + a- → -y a-.

sentences.t:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम् ।
यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः ॥
sentences.tr:
aho bata mahat pāpam kartum vyavasitāḥ vayam |
yat rājya-sukha-lobhena hantum sva-janam udyatāḥ ||

morph.gloss: to resolve (vyavasita: past participle 'resolved', nom. pl.; -āḥ before v- → -ā)
that, in that (yat: conjunction; -t + r- → -d r-)
greed (instr. sg.: 'out of greed for the pleasures of kingship')
to set out, be ready (udyata: past participle 'bent on', nom. pl.)

sentences.l: Ah, alas! a great evil to do we have resolved — we who, out of greed for the pleasures of kingship, to kill our own people are bent.
sentences.i: Alas, what a great sin we have set our minds to — ready to kill our own kin out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom!
sentences.n: Aho bata: two exclamations of dismay, one after the other. Vyavasitā vayam, 'we are resolved' — the perfect participle used as a past tense with the pronoun, a construction Sanskrit uses constantly instead of a finite verb. Yad here means 'in that, seeing that', introducing the reason for the dismay.

sentences.t:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत् ॥
sentences.tr:
yadi mām apratīkāram aśastram śastra-pāṇayaḥ |
dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ raṇe hanyuḥ tat me kṣemataram bhavet ||

morph.gloss: the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (nom. pl.; -āḥ before r- → -ā)
to kill (hanyuḥ: optative 3rd pl. 'should they kill'; -uḥ + t- → -us t-)
that (tat: nom. sg. neut.; -t + m- → -n m-)
better, safer (comparative of kṣema 'welfare'; nom. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: If me, unresisting, unarmed, the weapon-in-hand sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle should kill, that for me safer would be.
sentences.i: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me in battle, unarmed and unresisting, that would be better for me.
sentences.n: Two bahuvrīhis frame the verse: apratīkāram aśastram 'without resistance, without weapon' (Arjuna, accusative) against śastrapāṇayaḥ 'weapon-in-hand' (the Kauravas, nominative). Hanyuḥ is optative, 'should they kill'; bhavet, 'it would be' — the if-clause and its result both in the optative. Kṣemataram: the comparative -tara, 'more kṣema', more to my welfare.

sentences.t: सञ्जय उवाच
sentences.tr: sañjaya uvāca
sentences.l: Sañjaya said

morph.gloss: Sañjaya, the king's minister and charioteer, who reports the battle to him (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः संख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् ।
विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः ॥
sentences.tr:
evam uktvā arjunaḥ saṃkhye ratha-upasthe upāviśat |
visṛjya sa-śaram cāpam śoka-saṃvigna-mānasaḥ ||

morph.gloss: seat, lap (loc. sg. 'on the chariot-seat'; -a + u- → -o-; final -e stays before the vowel u-)
to sit down (upāviśat: imperfect 3rd sg. 'he sat down')
to let go, cast aside (visṛjya: gerund 'having cast aside')
arrow (saśaram: 'together with the arrow', acc. sg.)
mind (nom. sg. bahuvrīhi: 'his mind shaken by grief')

sentences.l: Thus having spoken, Arjuna, in the battle, on the chariot-seat sat down, having cast aside the arrow-and-bow, his-mind-shaken-with-grief.
sentences.i: Having spoken thus, in the midst of the battle Arjuna sank down on the seat of his chariot and let fall his bow and arrow, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
sentences.n: The narrator's voice returns for one verse. Rathopastha upāviśat: ratha + upastha gives rathopastha-, and the locative -e stays unchanged before the vowel u-, which is why it is written रथोपस्थ with no ending visible. Saśaraṃ cāpam, 'the bow with its arrow' — sa- 'with' prefixed to śara. The chapter ends on a bahuvrīhi, śoka-saṃvigna-mānasaḥ, 'whose mind is shaken by grief', and the teaching begins in chapter 2.

glossary.उत्साद्यन्ते: utsādyante — ut-sad — to abolish (utsādyante: causative passive 3rd pl. 'are abolished')
glossary.जातिधर्माः: jāti-dharmāḥ — jāti — birth-group, caste; dharma — law (nom. pl. 'the laws of caste')
glossary.कुलधर्माश्च: kula-dharmāḥ ca — kula — family; dharma — law (nom. pl.; -āḥ + c- → -āś c-); ca — and
glossary.उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां: utsanna-kula-dharmāṇām — utsanna — destroyed (past participle of ut-sad); kula — family; dharma — law (gen. pl. bahuvrīhi: 'of men whose family laws are destroyed')
glossary.मनुष्याणां: manuṣyāṇām — manuṣya — man, human being (gen. pl.)
glossary.नरकेऽनियतं: narake aniyatam — naraka — hell (loc. sg.); aniyata — indefinite, unending (adverbial acc. 'for an indefinite time'; -e + a- → -e ' with avagraha; see note for the variant niyatam)
glossary.वासो: vāsaḥ — vāsa — dwelling (nom. sg.; -aḥ before bh- → -o)
glossary.भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम: bhavati iti anuśuśruma — bhū — to be (bhavati: present 3rd sg.; -i + i- → -ī-); iti — thus (closes the reported statement; -i + a- → -y a-); anu-śru — to hear by tradition (anuśuśruma: perfect 1st pl. 'we have heard')
glossary.महत्पापं: mahat pāpam — mahat — great (acc. sg. neut.); pāpa — evil, sin (acc. sg.)
glossary.व्यवसिता: vyavasitāḥ — vi-ava-so — to resolve (vyavasita: past participle 'resolved', nom. pl.; -āḥ before v- → -ā)
glossary.यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन: yat rājya-sukha-lobhena — yad — that, in that (yat: conjunction; -t + r- → -d r-); rājya — kingship; sukha — pleasure; lobha — greed (instr. sg.: 'out of greed for the pleasures of kingship')
glossary.स्वजनमुद्यताः: sva-janam udyatāḥ — sva — own; jana — people (svajanam: acc. sg. 'kinsfolk'); ud-yam — to set out, be ready (udyata: past participle 'bent on', nom. pl.)
glossary.मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं: mām apratīkāram aśastram — aham — I (mām: acc. sg. 'me'); apratīkāra — not resisting, unresisting (acc. sg.); aśastra — unarmed, without weapon (acc. sg.)
glossary.शस्त्रपाणयः: śastra-pāṇayaḥ — śastra — weapon; pāṇi — hand (nom. pl. bahuvrīhi: 'weapon in hand')
glossary.धार्तराष्ट्रा: dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ — Dhārtarāṣṭra — the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (nom. pl.; -āḥ before r- → -ā)
glossary.हन्युस्तन्मे: hanyuḥ tat me — han — to kill (hanyuḥ: optative 3rd pl. 'should they kill'; -uḥ + t- → -us t-); tad — that (tat: nom. sg. neut.; -t + m- → -n m-); aham — I (me: enclitic gen./dat. 'for me')
glossary.क्षेमतरं: kṣemataram — kṣematara — better, safer (comparative of kṣema 'welfare'; nom. sg. neut.)
glossary.भवेत्: bhavet — bhū — to be (bhavet: optative 3rd sg. 'would be')
glossary.एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः: evam uktvā arjunaḥ — evam — thus; vac — to speak (uktvā: gerund 'having spoken'; -ā + a- → -ā-); Arjuna — Arjuna (nom. sg.)
glossary.संख्ये: saṃkhye — saṃkhya — battle (loc. sg. 'in the battle')
glossary.रथोपस्थ: ratha-upasthe — ratha — chariot; upastha — seat, lap (loc. sg. 'on the chariot-seat'; -a + u- → -o-; final -e stays before the vowel u-)
glossary.उपाविशत्: upāviśat — upa-viś — to sit down (upāviśat: imperfect 3rd sg. 'he sat down')
glossary.विसृज्य: visṛjya — vi-sṛj — to let go, cast aside (visṛjya: gerund 'having cast aside')
glossary.सशरं: sa-śaram — sa — with (prefix); śara — arrow (saśaram: 'together with the arrow', acc. sg.)
glossary.शोकसंविग्नमानसः: śoka-saṃvigna-mānasaḥ — śoka — grief; saṃvigna — agitated, shaken (past participle of sam-vij); mānasa — mind (nom. sg. bahuvrīhi: 'his mind shaken by grief')
